content_list.content_text: The 1970s began with the trial of Charles Manson for the murders that shook the Hollywood elite. The Watergate break-in permanently stained the highest office in the land, and the unpopular Vietnam War ended with the humiliating evacuation of American forces from Saigon. Like the era to which they belonged, crime films were characterized by disillusionment, distrust of authority, and paranoia.

content_list.content_text: Three of the era's classics denounce the nation's moral bankruptcy through the lens of history. Francis Ford Coppola (b. 1939) gave the world The Godfather (1972) and its sequel The Godfather Part II (1974) and, in doing so, reinvented the gangster film as grand opera. Both films place the Mafia squarely at the center of American life and, coincidentally, gave new meaning to one of the most American of concepts, "the family."

content_list.title: Building the Myth of the Mobster with The Godfather
content_list.description:
The youngest son, Michael Corleone (Al Pacino), returns from World War II outside the family business: organized crime. When his father, Don Corleone (Marlon Brando), is gunned down, however, Michael is driven to carry out a vendetta, a retaliatory killing, bound by blood and "honor" to a violent chain of events of power and survival in the underworld. Ultimately, Michael inherits the role of head of the family, shutting the door on his uncomprehending non-Italian wife (Diane Keaton) as he receives homage as the new "Godfather," or boss.

The film's dialogue and characters immediately entered the collective imagination of moviegoers. Al Pacino (b. 1940) and James Caan (b. 1940) (the hotheaded older brother Sonny) became stars, and the film won the Oscars for Best Picture and Best Screenplay, as well as Best Actor for Brando, in a triumphant comeback. In adapting Mario Puzo's bestseller, Francis Ford Coppola made a gangster opera in the pulp fiction style, an epic about patriarchy, family and America itself. Protests of defamation from Italian Americans were swept aside by the film's immense popularity. Every descendant of immigrants looked on with nostalgia at the Corleone clan making pasta, celebrating and grieving together. The anecdotes, footnotes and postscripts are now part of the folklore - Brando didn't stuff his cheeks with cotton but wore resin pads attached to his molars, and he sent a fake Native American, "Sacheen Littlefeather," to the Oscars ceremony to decline his award.

Coppola set many of the rules of the game for 1970s cinema with his technical mastery. The audacious, visceral and grandiose set pieces are now legendary - the horse's head in the bed, the slaughter of Sonny, the scenes cutting between a sunny garden wedding party and Don Corleone's entourage inside the house, and the stunning finale with murders being carried out during the baptism of the new Corleone (in effect, the rites of consecration for Michael as he assumes the role of the new boss). The film's best qualities reveal Coppola's fluency in the classics, in pulp, film noir and social dramas, but a persistent criticism of The Godfather is that it glorifies the Mafia. Pacino's Michael is the film's hero, and Michael is not a good guy. Even so, its mythic exploration of family ties, even when they are cursed by blood and ambition, keeps drawing viewers in with the idea that having a family (even a Mafia one) is still better than having no family at all.

content_list.content_text: Chinatown (1974), directed by Roman Polanski (b. 1933), also investigates the criminal foundations of American society, with a story of murder and incest that unfolds against a backdrop of endemic corruption during the growth of Los Angeles.

information.contentText: The film's opening scene is a long zoom out from the face of the character Bonasera, ending up behind Vito Corleone. The zoom, which lasts three minutes, was made with computer-controlled lenses created by Tony Karp.

content_list.content_text: Lack of faith in the law is the theme of many crime films of the era. Dirty Harry (1971), by director Don Siegel (1912-1991), features detective Harry Callahan, played by Clint Eastwood (b. 1930), doing as he pleases on the streets of San Francisco while hunting a sadistic serial killer.

quote.quote: The way the film was released, it was as if God had taken care of it.
quote.author: William Friedkin on The French Connection

content_list.content_text: This film is not an endorsement of vigilante justice (as its liberal critics claim). Its theme is the destructive synergy between the cop and the psychopath. In The French Connection (1971), director William Friedkin (b. 1935) presents the law in the form of Popeye Doyle, a charmless, foul-mouthed cop who contrasts with the polished, aristocratic kingpin he is trying to bring down. Based on true events, it shows the police and the criminals operating on a basis of moral equivalence.

information.contentText: Robert Towne's screenplay for the film has become legendary among critics and filmmakers, often celebrated as one of the best ever written. However, it was Polanski who decided on the tragic final scene, changing Towne's idea, as he had written a happy ending.

content_list.content_text: In The Long Goodbye (1973), by Robert Altman (1925-2006), private detective Philip Marlowe, a kind of knight-errant created by Raymond Chandler, is given a makeover for the 1970s. Elliott Gould's Marlowe is a man out of his time, chain-smoking in a Hollywood where a gangster's preferred method of extracting information is to stage an impromptu nudist encounter. Screenwriter Leigh Brackett (1915-1978) had worked on an earlier adaptation of Chandler's work, The Big Sleep (1946), and her screenplay for Altman captures the cadences of the 1970s cult of individualism.
In his essay The 'Me' Decade and the Third Great Awakening (1976), Tom Wolfe defined the solipsism of the era. He could just as well have been writing about the Los Angeles of The Long Goodbye.

information.contentText: Censored in many countries, Scarface was the first film in which the word "fuck" is used 226 times in total, with Tony Montana alone saying it 182 times. An old rumor claimed that the band Blink-182 took the 182 from the film, but this was later denied by the members, who said it was pure coincidence.

content_list.content_text: Clint Eastwood made his directorial debut with Play Misty for Me (1971), a film attuned to the dictates of the "Me" decade, transforming his screen persona: instead of an action hero, he plays a smug late-night radio disc jockey. A smooth-jazz-fueled seducer, he is stunned when the fan he carelessly takes to bed turns into a homicidal stalker.

content_list.title: The Revival of Mafia Films
content_list.description:
In the 1970s, there was a resurgence of mafia films, most notably The Godfather. It was followed by two sequels: The Godfather Part II (1974) and The Godfather Part III (1990), and it also inspired other mafia films, such as The Valachi Papers (1972).

The first Godfather film portrayed a dichotomy of values between the first-generation Italian-American Vito Corleone, who still follows the traditional mafioso code of honor, and his Americanized son Michael, who over the course of the films loses all his moral principles as greed consumes him. The Godfather films also offered a perverted version of the famous "American Dream," as the Corleones rose to power and wealth through entirely illegal and brutal means. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, events such as the Vietnam War and various social protest movements caused many Americans to lose faith in traditional American values, and so the distorted, dark version of the theme held particular appeal when the film was released in 1972. Inspired by the films' worldwide success in the 1970s, Italian films portrayed mafiosi as antiheroes, men who lived by crime but possessed a certain nobility and greatness of character.

The 1983 remake of Scarface, Scarface (1983), was not particularly well received at the time of its release, but over time it came to be seen as a classic of mafia films, serving as inspiration for films such as King of New York (1990). Sergio Leone (1929-1989) filmed an epic crime drama, Once Upon a Time in America (1984), starring Robert De Niro (b. 1943) and James Woods (b. 1947). Although the release of the "US Cut" was a commercial and critical failure, the releases of the "European Cut" and "Director's Cut" were both critical successes and restored its publicity and reputation. The Untouchables (1987), directed by Brian De Palma (b. 1940), presented a largely fictionalized version of Eliot Ness's efforts to enforce the law and bring down Al Capone's "Outfit."

The 1980s saw La Mattanza ("The Slaughter") in Italy, as the Corleonesi family wiped out its rivals, leading to more than 1,000 gang murders in 1981-83, and the Mafia also murdered magistrates, police officers, and journalists with impunity. In the 1980s and 1990s, the general feeling in Italy was that the Mafia was out of control. As a consequence, Italian cinema in the 1980s and 1990s turned to civil cinema, a series of realistic and courageous films that portrayed the Mafia as an unstoppable force that had completely corrupted almost everyone and murdered the few honest people willing to stand up to it. Films and TV series such as La piovra (1984), La scorta (1993), and Palermo-Milano sola andata (1995) had as their heroes a lone police officer or magistrate, the only one to cling to his honesty and integrity, who faced not only the Mafia's killers but also his corrupt superiors and the prevailing apathy of Italian society.

The following decade would continue with critically acclaimed mafia film productions, with Martin Scorsese leading most of the big hits, among them GoodFellas (1990).

content_list.content_text: The rise of Black consciousness in the 1970s was reflected in the blaxploitation phenomenon (exploitation of Black stereotypes), with films aimed at Black audiences. The tone for the genre was set by Shaft (1971) - directed by African American filmmaker Gordon Parks (1912-2006) and starring a charismatic detective - and by the more ambiguous Super Fly (1972), directed by Parks's son, Gordon Parks Jr. (1934-1979), with a ghetto drug dealer as its hero. Both films feature revolutionary soundtracks, as successful as the films themselves - Shaft, by Isaac Hayes (1942-2008), and Super Fly, by Curtis Mayfield (1942-1999).

information.contentTitle: Trailer for Once Upon a Time in America
information.contentText: It was the last film Leone directed before his death five years later and the first feature film he had directed in 13 years. The cinematography was by Tonino Delli Colli, and the film's score was by Ennio Morricone. Leone originally planned two three-hour films, then a single 269-minute version (4 hours and 29 minutes), but was persuaded by the distributors to cut it to 229 minutes (3 hours and 49 minutes). The film premiered on May 23, 1984, at the Cannes Film Festival in France and was released in a shortened 139-minute version (2 hours and 19 minutes) on June 1, 1984, in the United States. Although the original European release received positive reviews, the shortened version was a critical and commercial failure in the United States. The film is now generally recognized as a masterpiece and one of the greatest gangster films ever made.

content_list.content_text: In a decade that began with the trial of Charles Manson and witnessed the mass suicide of Jim Jones's cult, it was possible to believe the devil was on the loose, a mood well captured by the occult-tinged road movie Race with the Devil (1975). In this exercise in post-Manson paranoia, two couples on vacation in an RV witness a human sacrifice and are pursued by members of a devil-worshipping cult. It shows the American Southwest in the grip of a satanic conspiracy.

content_list.content_text: Although both the 1960s and the 1980s produced excellent crime films, the profusion of original works capturing the mood of the times made the 1970s the golden age of the genre. Despite the recent trend toward remaking classics, the DNA of 1970s crime thrillers has occasionally been used to create original works of superior quality.

movies.title: The Godfather
movies.overview: Spanning the years 1945 to 1955, a chronicle of the fictional Italian-American Corleone crime family. When organized crime family patriarch, Vito Corleone barely survives an attempt on his life, his youngest son, Michael steps in to take care of the would-be killers, launching a campaign of bloody revenge.

movies.title: Dirty Harry
movies.overview: When a madman dubbed 'Scorpio' terrorizes San Francisco, hard-nosed cop, Harry Callahan – famous for his take-no-prisoners approach to law enforcement – is tasked with hunting down the psychopath. Harry eventually collars Scorpio in the process of rescuing a kidnap victim, only to see him walk on technicalities. Now, the maverick detective is determined to nail the maniac himself.

movies.title: Chinatown
movies.overview: Private eye Jake Gittes lives off of the murky moral climate of sunbaked, pre-World War II Southern California. Hired by a beautiful socialite to investigate her husband's extra-marital affair, Gittes is swept into a maelstrom of double dealings and deadly deceits, uncovering a web of personal and political scandals that come crashing together.

movies.title: Shaft
movies.overview: Cool black private eye John Shaft is hired by a crime lord to find and retrieve his kidnapped daughter.

movies.title: Scarface
movies.overview: After getting a green card in exchange for assassinating a Cuban government official, Tony Montana stakes a claim on the drug trade in Miami. Viciously murdering anyone who stands in his way, Tony eventually becomes the biggest drug lord in the state, controlling nearly all the cocaine that comes through Miami. But increased pressure from the police, wars with Colombian drug cartels and his own drug-fueled paranoia serve to fuel the flames of his eventual downfall.

movies.title: The Godfather: Part II
movies.overview: In the continuing saga of the Corleone crime family, a young Vito Corleone grows up in Sicily and in 1910s New York. In the 1950s, Michael Corleone attempts to expand the family business into Las Vegas, Hollywood and Cuba.

movies.title: The French Connection
movies.overview: Tough narcotics detective 'Popeye' Doyle is in hot pursuit of a suave French drug dealer who may be the key to a huge heroin-smuggling operation.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in America
movies.original_title: Once Upon a Time in America
movies.overview: A former Prohibition-era Jewish gangster returns to the Lower East Side of Manhattan over thirty years later, where he once again must confront the ghosts and regrets of his old life.

movies.title: Play Misty for Me
movies.overview: A brief fling between a male disc jockey and an obsessed female fan takes a frightening, and perhaps even deadly turn when another woman enters the picture.

movies.title: The Untouchables
movies.overview: Young Treasury Agent Elliot Ness arrives in Chicago and is determined to take down Al Capone, but it's not going to be easy because Capone has the police in his pocket. Ness meets Jimmy Malone, a veteran patrolman and probably the most honorable one on the force. He asks Malone to help him get Capone, but Malone warns him that if he goes after Capone, he is going to war.
